panels.title: Playbook — what holds a shot together
items_html: Chain by job_id, not by adjective. To hold a face, a house or a wall across two shots, pass the earlier generation’s job as an extra reference and write “REFERENCE IMAGE N is the shot to reproduce” or “governs the wall, house, ground and background — reproduce them exactly.” Describing the same house again in prose drifts every single time.

Assign every reference a job in the first two lines. They arrive as REFERENCE IMAGE 1, 2, 3 in submission order. Say what each one controls and what it must not contribute — “composition and crop only, ignore its room, its colours, its text overlay.” An unassigned reference leaks its content into the render.

The unlit strand close-up is always REFERENCE IMAGE 1 on any shot with the curtain in it. It is the only thing that makes the product read as string lights rather than a screen. The anti-panel block in content/curtain_realism/ goes in verbatim alongside it — pasted, not paraphrased, not trimmed.

Different surface? Override the block, do not edit it. One line ahead of it: “SURFACE OVERRIDE: wherever the block says ‘garage door’, read ‘gable end siding wall’ — everything else applies exactly as written.” Rewriting the block itself is how it quietly stops working.

Empty space has to be described as an object. Clear sky for a text overlay, a bare sofa cushion, a wall with no windows — all of it renders only when written out positively and then fenced with a ban list: “nothing resting on it: no boxes, no bags, no blankets.” “An empty sofa” produces a full one.

“Switched off” renders as “absent”. An unlit curtain has to be described as hardware — dull cold-grey plastic beads, dark wires, sag, uneven hem — and given a light source to catch: a street lamp raking across it. Otherwise the model returns a bare wall.

Describe the grip, not the object. For anything held, say what each hand is doing and where the rest of the mass goes. “A dozen strands bundled and compressed together between her fingers” plus “pools on the snowy ground beside the step stool” reads; “holding the curtain” gives an empty hand.

No text on the artwork, ever — and the ban has to be loud. Left alone the model turns every gag into a caption spelled across the house. The line that holds: “NO TEXT, NO LETTERS, NO WORDS, NO NUMBERS, NO SIGNS anywhere in the light artwork or anywhere in the photo.”

Comedy as a situation, not a punchline. Santa with a beer, Santa raiding the fridge, a reindeer visibly fed up with waiting — these read from the street in chunky bulbs. Anything that needs reading, or that tips past cheeky into crude, does not survive as an ad.
Wall colour is a lighting decision. White bulbs vanish on near-black brick. Pale greige, cream or light siding is what makes the product visible at all — pick the surface before the scene.
Change one thing at a time. Feed the approved frame back, restate what must not move, then label the edit “CHANGE ONE THING ONLY”. Never rewrite a prompt that already worked.

Every prompt carries the look clause. “Hyper realistic, crisp real-estate-photography clarity, evenly exposed, sharp focus front to back… NOT cinematic, no colour grading, no vignette, no shallow depth of field, no bloom, no CGI polish.” Drop it and the frame turns into a movie still.

det.text:
A real vertical snapshot taken on an iPhone by an ordinary person standing in a snowy front yard. NOT a product photo, NOT an advertisement. Match the raw, imperfect, amateur look and vertical framing of the reference image: dark evergreen shrubs along the bottom, pale cream horizontal vinyl siding, black shutter and window at the left edge.

SCENE: A middle-aged man in a navy quilted vest over a grey hoodie, jeans and a brown cap, standing on the top step of a small aluminium ladder, arms stretched up, biting the end of a roll of silver duct tape while his other hand smooths a strip across the bottom edge of a large 55-inch flat black television taped to the siding. His full face is clearly visible to the camera, head up, not blocked by the box. Left side of frame: a light wood dresser with a small decorated Christmas tree glowing warm white and a lit table lamp with a cream shade. Right side: a curtain of warm white fairy lights hanging down the beige wall, a white power outlet. Beige carpet, beige walls, an ordinary lived-in bedroom with a few real everyday details. Lighting: warm lamp and tree light mixed with cool dusk from a window, believable direction and falloff, soft real shadows, nothing evenly lit, nothing glowing artificially. Sharp modern flagship phone photo quality, no filter, no cinematic colour grade, no orange tint, natural depth of field. An ordinary snapshot a real person took, not a render, not an advertisement. det.label: Clip prompt · v8_c05_g1.mp4
det.text:
Handheld vertical phone video out of a car side window at night, one continuous take, the car driving forward and closing in so the lit wall grows larger and nearer through the clip and never recedes, street and snow verge flowing past, slow pan to hold the wall in frame. Handheld micro-shake, real phone-camera look, slight sensor noise, no cinematic bokeh, no zoom.

THE ONE RULE THAT MATTERS MOST — THE WALL IS A TV SCREEN: the tall lit panel on the house wall behaves exactly like a giant flat television screen bolted flat onto the wall. Its picture is hard-cropped at the panel's four edges like at a TV bezel — no part of the animated figure, no arm, hand, drink, sandal, sunglasses flash, sparkle, glow, halo or light spill can EVER appear outside the panel rectangle. Everything outside that rectangle — the roof, the sky, the snow, the windows, the siding around the panel, the yard, the street — is completely dark and unlit, exactly as in the start image, and stays that way in every frame. The panel is the ONLY light source on the whole house. All motion inside the panel keeps a clear margin of dark wall between the artwork and the panel edges; anything reaching an edge is cut off at the edge like at a TV bezel. The figure never grows past the panel edges.

Inside the screen, the bearded figure lounging on the striped beach chair moves constantly and never freezes. Beat by beat: at 0 to 1 second he leans back deeper into the beach chair and takes a long sip from a drink with a tiny umbrella straw, cheeks hollowing; at 1 to 2 seconds he lowers his sunglasses with one finger and peeks over them at the viewer, eyebrows waggling; at 2 to 3 seconds he kicks his feet up and wiggles his bare toes while the chair rocks; at 3 to 4 seconds he throws his head back in a big laugh, belly bouncing, and raises the drink in a toast as the clip ends. Every pose change is rendered by bulbs switching on and off row by row across the grid like an animated light-bulb sign.

Look at this wall!" followed by an amazed laugh, voice close to the phone microphone the way a passenger sounds inside a car. Underneath: the low hum of the car interior and tires rolling on packed snow. NO music, no narration.

det.label: Image prompt · v8_c07_g1.png
det.text:
Vertical 9:16 real iPhone night video still, hyper-photorealistic, grainy dark areas, filmed handheld from across a snow-covered suburban street at night. Unedited phone-clip aesthetic.

COMPOSITION - MATCH EXACTLY: The huge flat gable-end wall of a large suburban house takes up the whole upper-left region of the frame - tan-orange brick on the lower half, pale cream siding on the upper half, absolutely no windows, the roof edge cutting a strong diagonal from the top-left toward the right. The wall's corner is roughly centre-frame, and past it the street continues into darkness. The wall is bare, dark and unlit.

THE TWO GIRLS: Centre of the frame at medium distance, two young women in their early twenties walking together along a snowy path toward the lower-right, three-quarter view, one slightly behind the other. Both hold phones up and look DOWN at the screens, which uplight their faces in a hard cold blue-white - clearly the brightest element in the picture. Left girl: cream knit beanie with a fluffy pom, black puffer jacket, off-white joggers, tan winter boots, long ash-blonde hair. Right girl: bare-headed, long dark brown hair, beige plaid blanket scarf, black wool coat, black jeans, brown boots. Both mid-stride, relaxed, entirely candid, neither aware of the camera. Real skin texture, no retouching, correct number of fingers on every hand.

THE GROUND: Thick snow over everything. A trampled snowy walkway with many boot prints crosses the middle of the frame, dropping over a low curb onto a snowy road in the foreground bottom third. A snow-crusted low hedge line runs along the foot of the house wall.

BACKGROUND RIGHT: Beyond the corner of the wall, a neighbouring house recedes into darkness with a couple of small warm-orange windows and a faint porch lamp, bare winter branches, deep navy night sky.

LIGHTING - CRITICAL: The scene is genuinely dark. NO Christmas lights, NO string lights, NO holiday decorations anywhere - the enormous wall is completely bare and unlit. Only light: the two phone screens on their faces plus faint distant windows. Cold blue-black night palette, deep shadow, snow reading pale blue.

QUALITY: Natural phone-camera low-light look, visible sensor noise, no cinematic grading, no HDR. NO text overlays, no captions, no watermark, no logos or brand names.

det.label: Clip prompt · v8_c07_g1.mp4
det.text:
The clip begins EXACTLY on the provided start frame, pixel-identical — the very first frame of the video IS the reference image itself, same two people in the same positions, same framing, same dark house wall; nothing is recomposed before the action starts.

Handheld phone video at night in the snow, vertical 9:16, one continuous 4 second shot, no cuts and no zoom.
The two people in heavy winter coats keep walking away down the snowy path, heads down over their phones. At 0.8 seconds the huge dark house wall behind them lights up all at once with an enormous animated Christmas display built from thousands of tiny LED bulbs — and it is playing a comedy: a big cartoon Santa sneaking on exaggerated tiptoe with a giant sack of presents over his shoulder trips over a candy cane, faceplants into a pixel snow pile with his boots flying up, and wrapped presents scatter everywhere in a burst. He pops back up with the empty sack stuck over his head, staggers in a circle, yanks it off, and shrugs at the viewer with a huge sheepish grin while a reindeer beside him doubles over slapping its knee, laughing. Red, green and white bulbs, bright and saturated, the display animating without stopping until the last frame — bulbs chasing in programmed sequence, every movement drawn frame by frame in the bulb grid.
The two people react like real people, natural and understated: they notice the glow on the snow around them, one lifts their head first, then the other a half-beat later. They slow to a stop mid-step and turn around on the spot to face the wall, looking up at it. One gives a short real laugh and nudges the other with an elbow, then they casually raise their phones and film the lit wall, relaxed, amused. No jumping, no jolting, no staggering backward — just an ordinary genuine double-take two real people would do. They stay there filming until the clip ends, colored light washing over their coats.
They keep the same faces, hair, hats and winter clothing as the first frame. The display stays flat and anchored on the wall with correct perspective, hard-clipped to the wall edges — no bulb, present or glow ever crosses the roofline, the sky or the snow, and no light spills off the wall. Bulbs crisp and individually visible, character proportions and colors consistent throughout. Real low light phone camera look with sensor noise. No text overlays and no watermark.
Audio: a short amused laugh from one of them, boots crunching in snow, quiet cold night ambience. No music and no narration.

3.5–5.0s — She grabs one LED CURTAIN LIGHTS box off the shelf with both hands, hugs it to her chest, and bounces on her feet laughing, extremely happy, turning halfway back toward the camera to show it. End frame: her hugging the box, beaming.

det.label: Clip prompt · v18_c02_g1.mp4
det.text:
Animate the reference image exactly as it is. The first frame of the video IS the reference image, unchanged. Same woman, same face, same strawberry-blonde hair, same oatmeal cable-knit jumper and grey joggers, same living room, same forest-green velvet sofa, same flocked tree, same warm lamp light.

CAMERA - HELD IPHONE, LOCKED FOCAL LENGTH, feet planted, natural hand shake only. ABSOLUTELY NO ZOOM, no punch-in, no push-in, no pull-back, no dolly, no orbit, no crane, no speed ramp, no slow motion, no cuts. Same framing at the end as at the start.

THIS ONE SHOT CONTAINS TWO BEATS BACK TO BACK: she sets the box down AND drops to her knees in ONE combined motion, and then immediately opens the lid. There is no pause and no cut between them.

BEAT ONE - SETTING IT DOWN AND KNEELING ARE THE SAME MOVEMENT. She does not put the box down first and then kneel. She does not kneel first and then put the box down. Her knees bend at the same time her arms lower, and the box touches the cushion at roughly the same moment her knees touch the floor.
0.0-1.2s - she sinks straight down, knees bending, torso staying upright, while her arms extend forward and lower the big matt-black LED CURTAIN LIGHTS box toward the seat cushion. Box and body descend together in one smooth continuous arc. The box settles flat onto the seat cushion at the same instant her knees come to rest on the floor in front of the sofa; the cushion compresses slightly under the weight.

BEAT TWO - SHE OPENS IT, KNEELING.
1.2-1.9s - now kneeling at the sofa, she squares the box up on the cushion, gets a fingertip under the front edge of the magnetic lid and gives it a small tug; the magnet releases with a tiny snap.
1.9-3.1s - one-handed, she pivots the big printed lid UP and BACK on its hinge, keeping the printed face turned toward the camera as it swings, until it stands open at roughly seventy degrees. Real cardboard weight - the lid does not come off, does not detach and does not fold flat instantly.
3.1-4.0s - the open box reveals the neatly folded dense black LED curtain mesh inside. She reaches in with her other hand, lifts the top edge of the mesh slightly, feels it, then turns her head toward the camera with a delighted smile, chest rising with a quick excited breath. Small natural movement throughout - nothing ever freezes.

HARD RULES:
- The box ends up ON THE SEAT CUSHION. It never touches the floor.
- She ends up on her knees on the floor in front of the sofa, not sitting on it.
- The LED lights stay COMPLETELY OFF and dark the entire time. Nothing inside the box glows. Nothing is lifted out of the box.
- The lid stays attached and stays printed-side toward camera. Do not redesign the packaging - the printing stays rigid, sharp and correctly spelled as the lid rotates.
- Identity lock: same face, same hair, same clothes, same room, same sofa, same framing.
- No cuts, no text, no captions, no logos, no on-screen graphics, no watermark.

AUDIO: quiet room tone, the soft thump of a heavy box landing on a cushion, knees on the floor, the magnetic lid snapping open, cardboard flex, soft fabric rustle, a small delighted breath. NO music, NO narration.

LOOK: real iPhone UGC footage, natural warm indoor light, slight sensor noise, not cinematic, not colour graded, no slow motion.

det.text:

REAL TIME — NORMAL 1x SPEED. THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT RULE IN THIS PROMPT. This is one real-time phone video played back at ordinary speed. Everything happens at the pace a real person actually moves: she walks at a walking pace, she kneels at the speed a body really kneels, the lid swings open at the speed heavy cardboard really swings. ABSOLUTELY NO fast motion, NO sped-up playback, NO double speed, NO under-cranking, NO time-lapse, NO hyperlapse, NO sudden jump in tempo, NO frantic twitchy limbs, NO snapping instantly from one pose to the next, NO scrubbing through the action. There is DELIBERATELY very little to do in five seconds — one slow lowering, one slow kneel, one slow lid. If the action does not fit comfortably, SLOW THE ACTION DOWN; never speed the footage up. It is far better that she is still settling as the clip ends than that any part of it looks fast-forwarded.

REFERENCE IMAGES. Reference image 1 is the first frame of scene 1 — start there, unchanged, and it owns the room, the camera angle and the geometry. Reference image 2 is the CLOSED PRODUCT BOX: the artwork on the box in this video must match it exactly. Reference image 3 is the OPEN BOX INTERIOR: what she reveals in scene 2 must match it exactly.

BOX SPEC — TRUE IN EVERY FRAME. A matte black rigid retail box, 55 cm wide x 42 cm tall x 10 cm deep. It is BIG — much wider than the span of two outstretched hands; each of her hands covers less than a quarter of the box width, and laid on the sofa seat it spans most of one cushion. Front panel top to bottom: a large white condensed uppercase headline LED CURTAIN LIGHTS; a warm gold subline Create Your Own Magic; a red diagonal BEST SELLER ribbon flag in the top-right corner; one large photographic panel with a thin gold hairline border showing a night house facade with a glowing pixel LED Christmas tree on the garage door; a bottom row of five small gold line icons with white captions. NO transparent window, NO clear plastic panel, NO die-cut cutout, NO product visible through the front, NO glowing lights showing through the cardboard. The box is closed and sealed until the moment she opens it in scene 2.

SCENE 1 — 0.0 to 2.5s. CAMERA: HELD IPHONE, LOCKED FOCAL LENGTH, portrait, a friend filming from above head height over her left shoulder and angled down, exactly where the reference image was taken. NO ZOOM IN, NO ZOOM OUT, NO PUSH IN, NO DOLLY. Handheld micro-shake only. She is at the LEFT EDGE of frame, partly cut off by it; the green velvet sofa is directly IN FRONT of her, running diagonally away into depth and filling the right and bottom-right of frame. The room behind her — the lit Christmas tree, the lamp, the wall and the floor — stays exactly as it is and never changes.
THE WHOLE POINT OF SCENE 1: she carries the box round in front of the sofa, sets it flat on the seat cushion AND drops to her knees IN THE SAME CONTINUOUS MOTION. These are not two separate steps — the box going down and her body going down are one move.
0.0-0.9s — one unhurried step forward and to her right, her shoulders turning, the heavy box swinging slowly out in front of her; her honey-blonde hair swings across and settles, her dusty-rose ribbed knit sleeve creases with the weight.
0.9-1.8s — she steps in front of the sofa and leans forward from the hips, lowering the box steadily toward the empty green velvet seat cushion, arms extending, knees already bending underneath her. This lowering is SLOW and heavy — the box is big and awkward and she is being careful with it.
1.8-2.5s — the box settles flat and printed-side-up on the cushion with a soft compression of the velvet, her hands still on it, and in the same continuous motion her knees come down onto the floor one after the other, her weight settling and her back rounding forward; she pushes her hair behind one ear and plants both palms flat on the box lid, chest rising with one excited breath.

HARD CUT AT 2.5s.

SCENE 2 — 2.5 to 5.0s. Direct continuation, same room, same second, same woman, same dusty-rose ribbed knit, same box in exactly the same place on the same green velvet cushion. The camera has moved about 30 degrees round to her side — a slightly more side-on three-quarter angle, a little lower, closer to the level of the sofa seat, so we now see the lid edge in profile and read the pivot clearly. Still HELD IPHONE, LOCKED FOCAL LENGTH, handheld micro-shake only, NO ZOOM.

The lid pivots UP and BACK on that hinge, rotating away from her and toward the back of the sofa, keeping its printed front face turned toward the camera as it rises. The inside of the lid is matte black. The lid is NEVER lifted off, NEVER removed, NEVER carried aside, NEVER set down, NEVER folded flat instantly, NEVER slid out like a drawer.
2.5-3.1s — she hooks her fingertips under the near front edge of the lid; a small snap as the magnets release and the front edge lifts a centimetre, a thin black shadow line opening slowly across the whole 55 cm width.
3.1-4.3s — she pivots the big printed lid UP and BACK on its hinge in ONE slow continuous arc with real cardboard weight, her elbows rising and her shoulders lifting with the effort, until it stands roughly vertical. 4.3-5.0s — the interior is revealed exactly as reference image 3: the neatly folded black LED mesh curtain in its tray with the coiled lead and the small accessory items. She reaches in with both hands and touches the folded mesh, fingers spreading it slightly, then lifts her chin, looks off toward the Christmas tree and breaks into a big open-mouthed grin, eyebrows up.

HARD RULES: exactly ONE cut, at 2.5s. The box never changes size, never changes artwork, never gains a window or a cutout. Nobody else enters frame. NO TEXT, NO LETTERS, NO WORDS, NO NUMBERS, NO CAPTIONS, NO SUBTITLES, NO WATERMARK anywhere in the video.

det.html:
File name

The old board listed v21_c02_g2.mp4 as the clip in the cut and marked it lost. This take is on disk as v21_c02_g1.mp4: its Higgsfield job carries the same clip prompt and its frames match the export (checked 2026-09-23). The 2026-09-18 naming migration left it under the earlier take number.

What made it work

State the camera as a sentence of its own, at the top, and repeat it as a negative. “COPY THE CAMERA AND STAGING OF REFERENCE IMAGE 1 EXACTLY. This is the most important instruction.” followed by “Do not move the camera to the side, do not shoot her from the front, do not put the sofa behind her.” Describing the sofa’s position relative to her (“DIRECTLY IN FRONT OF HER, filling the right half and the bottom-right, running diagonally away”) is what fixed it.

Regenerate without breaking a chain. Passing take 1’s own job back in as a reference kept the woman identical, so the already-approved C3 stayed valid.

What made it work

Speed is a structure problem, not an adjective problem. Piling on “slowly”, “unhurried” and “no fast motion” does nothing while the timeline still asks for three things. The fix was to delete a whole beat and stretch the two survivors to 2.0s each, then add a paragraph that says out loud why the deleted beat is missing: “THAT IS THE WHOLE CLIP… cramming it in is exactly what would force the footage to look sped up.”

“A clearly different pose every half second” is itself a speed-up instruction. That line was in every take-1 prompt and it is what taught the model to snap between poses. It was replaced with a continuous-but-unhurried rule: always moving, never hurried, every change flowing into the next at natural human speed.

Give it permission to end mid-action. “It is far better that she is still mid-reach as the clip ends than that any part of it looks fast-forwarded” removes the model’s incentive to compress, because finishing the action is no longer the goal.

If a pose would take a limb or the sack out to an edge, THE POSE IS MADE SMALLER so it stays inside — the rectangle is never made bigger to fit him. There is no lit bulb, no glow and no star anywhere above the roof edge or off the side of the wall. The wall and roof outside the curtain stay dark all four seconds.
PERSPECTIVE VS SCALE. As the car drives closer the lit rectangle naturally fills more of the CAMERA FRAME — that is correct. But the artwork never changes size relative to the wall it hangs on, and the wall never changes shape. The grid simply gets coarser and the bulbs bigger and more countable.

CAMERA — HANDHELD VERTICAL PHONE VIDEO SHOT OUT OF A MOVING CAR SIDE WINDOW AT NIGHT. THE CAR IS DRIVING FORWARD and closing in on the house, so the gable wall grows steadily and continuously LARGER across the four seconds and NEVER recedes. Real vehicle motion: the road surface and the snow verge flow past the bottom of frame at speed, roadside objects sweep past with strong parallax, the frame rocks gently with the suspension. As the car advances the operator slowly pans right to hold the lit wall in frame. THIS IS DRIVING, NOT ZOOMING: no focal length change, no digital zoom, no gimbal glide, no drone move.

HARD NEGATIVE — NO PHONE IN SHOT. There is no phone, no screen, no hand, no fingers, no thumb, no arm, no sleeve, no glove and no device anywhere in the foreground. Only the car's own dark window frame and wing mirror, exactly as in the reference image, sit at the bottom-left.

MOVEMENT — the animation is already ON and running at full speed in the very first frame and is STILL running in the last. A CLEARLY DIFFERENT POSE EVERY HALF SECOND, the figure fully redrawing between beats like an animated light-bulb sign:
0.0-1.0s — Santa takes a big exaggerated stride ON THE SPOT, his feet never leaving the centre of the curtain, his front boot swinging right forward and his back leg stretching out behind, the heavy red sack swinging out wide behind his shoulder and his beard flying back.
1.0-2.0s — he heaves the sack across to his other shoulder in one big two-handed swing, his body twisting, then throws his now-free arm up and waves broadly, hat tassel whipping across.
2.0-3.0s — the green wreath at the left swings and rocks on its hook, and every gold star around him twinkles out and back in a rolling wave from left to right while Santa takes two more striding steps on the spot.
3.0-4.0s — he stops, plants both boots, tips his hat forward with one hand in a big bow, beard bouncing, then straightens up and throws both arms out wide, mouth open in a huge laugh.
Every pose change is rendered by bulbs switching on and off row by row across the grid — chunky and instantaneous, never smooth morphing, never a crossfade. The coloured reflections on the wet road shift and streak with every change.

CRITICAL — HOW THE LIGHTS MUST BE BUILT. SURFACE OVERRIDE: wherever the block below says "garage door", read "the gable end wall of the house". Everything else in the block applies exactly as written.
The picture on the garage door is NOT an LED video wall, NOT a screen, NOT a projection. It is a hanging curtain of LED string lights: many thin vertical wires hung side by side from a header cable, each wire carrying small round bulbs. Build the whole picture out of VERTICAL DOTTED LINES OF LIGHT. The horizontal gap between neighbouring strands is visibly WIDER than the vertical gap between bulbs on the same strand, so the grid is tall and rectangular — never a square pixel matrix.
The curtain is SEE-THROUGH. Through the gaps between strands you clearly read the wall behind it: its seams, its trim, the faint shadows of the wires falling on it. The unlit areas are NOT a solid coloured field — they are simply dark wall, with the unlit bulbs showing as tiny dull grey dots and the thin dark wires as faint vertical lines.
Every lit bulb is a tiny point source: blown-out white core, coloured halo bleeding around it, a small soft star flare, individually countable. The artwork is extremely low resolution and blocky — chunky stepped edges, no smooth curves, no thin outlines, no small facial detail, no gradients, no anti-aliasing.
The curtain hangs a few inches proud of the wall: the strands sag slightly, each strand ends at a slightly different height so the bottom hem is uneven and wavy, a faint breeze tilts the sheet, and the glow bounces back off the wall behind it as a soft halo. Light spills onto the snow in a speckled uneven pattern, not a flat even wash.
ABSOLUTELY NO: LED video wall, TV screen, monitor, jumbotron, projector image, black backing panel, bezel or frame, dense square pixel grid, solid saturated background field, smooth clean vector artwork. Real amateur photo, natural noise, no CGI polish.

ABSOLUTE HARD RULE — REPEATING THE CONTAINMENT RULE BECAUSE IT IS THE ONE THING MOST LIKELY TO GO WRONG. The lit rectangle is hard-cropped at all four edges like a bezel. It NEVER grows, shrinks, shifts, warps or drifts on the wall. Santa marches ON THE SPOT and stays centred with dark wall visible all the way round him; he never walks sideways across the curtain, never strides out of it, and never scales up. No limb, no sack, no wreath and no star crosses the roof edge, the trim or the corner of the wall. Nothing spills onto the roof, the sky, the verge, the snow or the neighbouring houses. As the car gets closer the bulb grid simply becomes coarser and the individual bulbs bigger and more countable — the artwork does not gain detail and does not gain size.

HARD RULES: no people and no other vehicles enter the frame. NO TEXT, NO LETTERS, NO WORDS, NO NUMBERS, NO SIGNS anywhere in the light artwork, and no captions, subtitles or watermark anywhere in the video.

AUDIO: natural room sound only — no music, no score, no background song. Tyres on wet road, a low engine hum, cold air rushing past the open window, a faint electrical hum from the lights. No voice.

LOOK: real iPhone UGC at night from a car. Noisy shadows, blown highlights around the bulbs, slight rolling-shutter wobble, no cinematic grade, no lens flare, no slow motion, no speed ramp.

rows.why_html: job a19dbda9 — Same pixelated, low-energy artwork as C5 take 1, and the curtain only covered part of the gable with bare wall showing around it.

det.html:
File name

The old board listed v21_c07_g2.mp4 as the clip in the cut and marked it lost. This take is on disk as v21_c07_g1.mp4: its Higgsfield job carries the same clip prompt and its frames match the export (checked 2026-09-23). The 2026-09-18 naming migration left it under the earlier take number.

What made it work

“Covers the wall” has to be spelled out as coverage. “THE LED CURTAIN COVERS THE ENTIRE GABLE WALL — edge to edge, corner to corner, all the way up into the peak of the gable and all the way down to the ground. No bare wall left showing around it.”

One character beats a busy scene at this distance. A single big Santa with a sack and a wreath reads instantly from across the street; the multi-element scenes turn to mush once the bulb grid coarsens.

What made it work

The lit rectangle has to be described as a cage, not as a picture. Naming every part that could escape — paw, ear, end of the string, scarf — and saying that each one is forbidden from touching an edge works far better than one blanket “stays inside”.

Tell it which way to resolve the conflict. “If a pose would take a limb out to an edge, THE POSE IS MADE SMALLER — the rectangle is never made bigger to fit it.” Without that sentence the model grows the curtain instead of shrinking the drawing.

det.label: Image prompt · v22_c01_g6.png
det.text:
One reference image. @Image 1 is the exact photo to reproduce - same man, same face, same clothes, same sad ugly old Christmas decorations, same house wall, same weather, same light, same amateur vertical phone-photo look.

CHANGE ONE THING ONLY: MOVE THE CAMERA MUCH CLOSER TO THE MAN AND THE WALL. The camera is now standing only two or three steps away from him instead of far back across the yard. The man fills a large part of the frame - roughly from his waist up to above his head - and the pathetic old decorations he is wrestling with, and the patch of wall he is working on, read BIG and clearly legible. det.label: Clip prompt · v22_c01_g2.mp4
det.text:
Animate the reference image exactly as it is. The first frame of the video IS the reference image, unchanged — same duck-egg-blue clapboard wall, same white painted fascia and trim board along the top, same huge weathered plywood Santa cut-out with its paint flaking and splitting, same rusty tin star up at the left, same brittle dead garland strung along the top, same orange extension cord snaking across the bottom left, same aluminium step ladder, same man in the olive work jacket, grey joggers and grey fingerless gloves standing on the step ladder with a staple gun raised to the white trim.

CAMERA — HELD IPHONE, LOCKED FRAMING. One single continuous handheld vertical shot, a friend filming from a few steps away at roughly chest height, exactly the framing of the reference image. NO zoom in, NO zoom out, NO push-in, NO pull-back, NO pan, NO tilt, NO dolly, NO orbit, NO cuts, NO slow motion, NO speed ramp. The wall, the Santa cut-out, the ladder and the man all stay exactly the same size in frame from the first frame to the last. Handheld micro-shake only — a few pixels of organic drift, plus a tiny sympathetic jolt on each hard staple-gun recoil.

THE TOOL, MECHANICALLY — THIS IS THE PART THAT MUST LOOK REAL. He is holding a HEAVY-DUTY MANUAL SQUEEZE-HANDLE STAPLE GUN (a hand tacker): a compact steel and plastic body about the length of his hand, with a long lever handle running along the top that he squeezes DOWN into his palm, and a flat metal nose at the front where the staple comes out. It is not powered, it has no hose, no cable, no battery, no trigger guard, no barrel.
HOW HE FIRES IT, EVERY SINGLE TIME, WITHOUT EXCEPTION:
1. He places the FLAT NOSE of the gun in FULL FLAT CONTACT with the white trim board, pressed hard against the wood. The nose never leaves the surface while he fires. He NEVER fires into the air, never fires with a gap between the nose and the wood, never waves the gun around while squeezing, never points it at nothing.
2. His gloved fingers wrap OVER the top lever and his thumb sits along the side of the body. He squeezes the whole lever down into his palm with his forearm braced and his wrist straight and locked in line with his forearm. The squeeze is a short, hard, committed movement of the whole hand, not a dainty finger twitch.
3. On firing the gun BUCKS back into his palm — the body kicks up and back a couple of centimetres, his wrist and elbow absorb it, his shoulder jolts, and the nose skids a few millimetres on the wood before he presses it back down. A real staple appears flush in the trim under the nose.
4. Between shots he lifts the gun clear, repositions the nose a hand's width along the trim, presses it flat again, and only then squeezes. Reposition, press, squeeze, kick — every time.
NEGATIVES ON THE TOOL: no visible staple flying through the air, no sparks, no smoke, no muzzle flash, no recoil like a firearm, no laser, no hose, no cord attached to the gun, no gun floating, no gun changing size or shape between shots, no gun passing through the wood or through his hand, no second gun, and it never swaps hands. His hands have five normal fingers and stay attached to normal wrists. He keeps his other hand or forearm physically braced against the plywood or the trim at all times — he is always in real contact with something.
BODY WEIGHT IS REAL. He is standing on an aluminium step ladder: his boots stay ON the rungs, his weight is carried by his legs, the ladder takes his load and flexes and rocks under him. He leans, he counterbalances, he grabs. Nothing about him floats or glides.

HE IS ANGRY AND THOROUGHLY PISSED OFF. This is a man losing a fight with a piece of ugly Christmas decoration. Jaw clenched, eyebrows down and pulled together, nostrils flaring, teeth showing, muttering and swearing under his breath with his mouth working the whole time. His frustration escalates across the five seconds — he starts irritated and ends furious.

ACTION TIMELINE (5 seconds, one continuous take, no cuts):
0.0-1.0s — he presses the top corner of the big plywood Santa hard up against the white trim with his left forearm, shoulder driving into it, then sets the flat nose of the staple gun against the white trim, presses it hard into the wood and squeezes the lever down into his palm — one loud CRACK, the gun bucking back into his hand, his wrist and shoulder absorbing the kick, a staple left flush in the trim. His jaw sets, his eyebrows drive down.
1.0-2.0s — the Santa immediately sags and slides down out of position on that side, dry paint flaking off in a shower of chips. He snaps his head round to look at it, mouth twisting, and mutters a furious word; he shoves the panel back up with a hard two-handed heave, the plywood flexing and knocking against the clapboard.
2.0-3.0s — he pins it with his shoulder and fires THREE times in a row — nose pressed flat, squeeze, CRACK, kick; lift, shift a hand's width along the trim, press flat, squeeze, CRACK, kick; again — CRACK — his wrist and shoulder absorbing each kick, his face contorting, teeth bared, breath fogging; the brittle dead garland above him shakes loose a few needles with each hit.
3.0-4.0s — the bottom edge of the cut-out swings out and clips his knee; he flinches, his boot slips a rung on the step ladder and the ladder legs scrape and rock on the ground; he grabs the trim to steady himself, eyes screwed shut for an instant, then glares straight at the Santa and shouts one short silent word at it, shoulders high round his ears.
4.0-5.0s — he slams the nose flat against the trim and squeezes twice more, harder than necessary, the gun bucking hard into his palm each time, then yanks the panel square with one violent jerk, drops his gun hand to his side, and stands there breathing hard, chest heaving, staring up at the crooked flaking Santa with pure contempt, head shaking slowly side to side.

MOVEMENT RULE: a clearly different whole-body pose every half second. His FACE fully redraws between beats — eyebrows, eyes and mouth completely different shapes from one beat to the next. Jacket creases, gloves flex, the ladder rocks, the plywood flexes, paint chips fall.

HARD RULES: he is never hurt and there is no blood — this is comic frustration, not an accident. He never turns to smile at the camera and never speaks to it. Nobody else enters frame. The Santa cut-out stays weathered, flaking and ugly — it never gets repaired, repainted or straightened properly. NOT ONE light is lit anywhere in the shot. DO NOT CHANGE the blue clapboard, the white trim, the rusty tin star, the dead garland, the orange extension cord, the step ladder or the flat daylight exposure. NO TEXT, NO LETTERS, NO WORDS, NO NUMBERS, NO CAPTIONS, NO SUBTITLES, NO WATERMARK anywhere in the video.

AUDIO: natural room sound only — no music, no score, no background song. Sharp loud staple-gun cracks, plywood knocking and flexing against clapboard, dry paint flaking, an aluminium step ladder scraping and rocking, gloves gripping, his angry frustrated grunting and muttering and hard breathing. No clean dialogue, no narration, nobody else speaks.

LOOK: real iPhone UGC. Flat overcast winter daylight, slightly cool white balance, mild sensor noise, mild rolling-shutter wobble on the recoils, no bokeh, no cinematic grade, no lens flare, no slow motion, no speed ramp, no fast motion. Real physical weight in every contact — the plywood is heavy, the ladder is rigid, the gun is solid steel. Nothing looks weightless, rubbery, floaty or animated.

rows.why_html: job 80b0322b — Built on the v21 C1 camera — ground level, steep upward tilt, a blow-mould Santa on the roof ridge. The camera sits right across the yard, so the decorations are too small to read the gag.
job f337dfc3 — The v12 C1 camera — extension ladder, half-deflated mildewed inflatable Santa. Same distance problem, and the man sits so high in the frame there is nowhere to put the headline.

job b7640fa3 — The v5 camera — step ladder, homemade plywood Santa. This is the scene that got picked, but the roofline and gutter run straight through the top of the frame, so there is no clean band for text.
job da00a6ec — g3 re-shot with the camera lower and tilted up. The empty sky band at the top finally worked — but the camera was still parked across the yard.
job bcb3800a — g3 pulled back further so the action would sit low in the frame. Wrong direction: the man and the decorations shrank to nothing.
job fc3998a4 — The product was handled wrong — the curtain behaved like a stiff prop rather than a tangled net, and the whole shot read as obviously fake.

det.html:
What made it work

Name the empty space as an object. “Leave room for text” does nothing. “The TOP FIFTH OF THE FRAME IS CLEAN EMPTY OVERCAST SKY with nothing in it — not the roof, not the gutter, not a branch, not a wire” survives even a big camera move.

One change per generation. g6 attaches g4 and says “CHANGE ONE THING ONLY: MOVE THE CAMERA MUCH CLOSER”, then explicitly re-locks the pose, the decorations, the house and the weather. Five takes of re-describing the scene got nowhere; one take of naming the single change landed it.

What made it work

Write the curtain as strands, never as a surface. Vertical dotted lines of light, wider gaps sideways than up-and-down, see-through to the wall behind, uneven wavy hem. The moment it is allowed to be a flat sheet it renders as an LED video wall and the shot dies.

cards.title: Box over the sofa
cards.desc: Camera raised over her left shoulder, angled down. She holds the box out in mid-air over the empty dove-grey sofa seat that sits directly in front of her, about to drop it.

items.note_html: v21 C2 — the whole photo, reproduced exactly. Camera, angle, crop, distance, her position and pose, the sofa placement and the box height all stay; only the woman and the room change. · media ee0e6434

det.label: Image prompt · v22_c02_g6.png
det.text:
@Image 1 is the photo. Keep it EXACTLY as it is. Same camera, same angle, same crop, same distance, same position and pose of the woman, same position and placement of the couch, same position and size of the box in her hands. Nothing about the framing moves.

CHANGE ONLY TWO THINGS:
1. A DIFFERENT WOMAN - different face, different hair, different outfit. She stands in exactly the same place, in exactly the same pose, holding the box exactly the same way.
2. A DIFFERENT ROOM - different wall, different couch colour and fabric, different decor and different Christmas tree. The couch stays in exactly the same place in the frame, at exactly the same angle and the same size.

Everything else is identical to @Image 1. Real amateur vertical iPhone photo, no text, no logos, no watermark.

det.label: Clip prompt · v22_c02_g2.mp4
det.meta: seedance_2_5 · 720p · 5 s · 9:16 · audio on · job d291f02d
det.text:
TWO SCENES IN ONE CLIP, JOINED BY ONE HARD CUT AT EXACTLY 2.5s. No dissolve, no fade, no whip pan, no transition effect — a straight in-camera cut, exactly like a creator cutting two takes together.

REAL TIME — NORMAL 1x SPEED. THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT RULE IN THIS PROMPT. This is one real-time phone video played back at ordinary speed. Everything happens at the pace a real person actually moves: she walks at a walking pace, she kneels at the speed a body really kneels, the lid swings open at the speed heavy cardboard really swings. ABSOLUTELY NO fast motion, NO sped-up playback, NO double speed, NO under-cranking, NO time-lapse, NO hyperlapse, NO sudden jump in tempo, NO frantic twitchy limbs, NO snapping instantly from one pose to the next, NO scrubbing through the action. There is DELIBERATELY very little to do in five seconds — one slow lowering, one slow kneel, one slow lid. If the action does not fit comfortably, SLOW THE ACTION DOWN; never speed the footage up. It is far better that she is still settling as the clip ends than that any part of it looks fast-forwarded.

REFERENCE IMAGES. Reference image 1 is the first frame of scene 1 — start there, unchanged, and it owns the room, the camera angle and the geometry. Reference image 2 is the CLOSED PRODUCT BOX: the artwork on the box in this video must match it exactly. Reference image 3 is the OPEN BOX INTERIOR: what she reveals in scene 2 must match it exactly.

BOX SPEC — TRUE IN EVERY FRAME. A matte black rigid retail box, 55 cm wide x 42 cm tall x 10 cm deep. It is BIG — much wider than the span of two outstretched hands; each of her hands covers less than a quarter of the box width, and laid on the sofa seat it spans most of one cushion. Front panel top to bottom: a large white condensed uppercase headline LED CURTAIN LIGHTS; a warm gold subline Create Your Own Magic; a red diagonal BEST SELLER ribbon flag in the top-right corner; one large photographic panel with a thin gold hairline border showing a night house facade with a glowing pixel LED Christmas tree on the garage door; a bottom row of five small gold line icons with white captions. NO transparent window, NO clear plastic panel, NO die-cut cutout, NO product visible through the front, NO glowing lights showing through the cardboard. The box is closed and sealed until the moment she opens it in scene 2.

SCENE 1 — 0.0 to 2.5s. CAMERA: HELD IPHONE, LOCKED FOCAL LENGTH, portrait, a friend filming from above head height over her left shoulder and angled down, exactly where the reference image was taken. NO ZOOM IN, NO ZOOM OUT, NO PUSH IN, NO DOLLY. Handheld micro-shake only. She is at the LEFT EDGE of frame, partly cut off by it; the pale cream sofa is directly IN FRONT of her, running diagonally away into depth and filling the right and bottom-right of frame. The room behind her — the lit Christmas tree, the lamp, the wall and the floor — stays exactly as it is and never changes.
THE WHOLE POINT OF SCENE 1: she carries the box round in front of the sofa, sets it flat on the seat cushion AND drops to her knees IN THE SAME CONTINUOUS MOTION. These are not two separate steps — the box going down and her body going down are one move.
0.0-0.9s — one unhurried step forward and to her right, her shoulders turning, the heavy box swinging slowly out in front of her; her dark chestnut hair swings across and settles, her cream cable-knit sleeve creases with the weight.
0.9-1.8s — she steps in front of the sofa and leans forward from the hips, lowering the box steadily toward the empty cream seat cushion, arms extending, knees already bending underneath her, her jeans creasing at the knee. This lowering is SLOW and heavy — the box is big and awkward and she is being careful with it.
1.8-2.5s — the box settles flat and printed-side-up on the cushion with a soft compression of the cushion, her hands still on it, and in the same continuous motion her knees come down onto the floor one after the other, her weight settling and her back rounding forward; she pushes her hair behind one ear and plants both palms flat on the box lid, chest rising with one excited breath.

HARD CUT AT 2.5s.

SCENE 2 — 2.5 to 5.0s. Direct continuation, same room, same second, same woman, same cream cable-knit and jeans, same box in exactly the same place on the same cream cushion. The camera has moved about 30 degrees round to her side — a slightly more side-on three-quarter angle, a little lower, closer to the level of the sofa seat, so we now see the lid edge in profile and read the pivot clearly. Still HELD IPHONE, LOCKED FOCAL LENGTH, handheld micro-shake only, NO ZOOM.
LID MECHANISM, GEOMETRICALLY. The box is a magnetic-closure flip-top. The hinge runs along the TOP LONG EDGE of the box — the far edge away from her, at the back. The lid pivots UP and BACK on that hinge, rotating away from her and toward the back of the sofa, keeping its printed front face turned toward the camera as it rises. The inside of the lid is matte black. The lid is NEVER lifted off, NEVER removed, NEVER carried aside, NEVER set down, NEVER folded flat instantly, NEVER slid out like a drawer.
2.5-3.1s — she hooks her fingertips under the near front edge of the lid; a small snap as the magnets release and the front edge lifts a centimetre, a thin black shadow line opening slowly across the whole 55 cm width.
3.1-4.3s — she pivots the big printed lid UP and BACK on its hinge in ONE slow continuous arc with real cardboard weight, her elbows rising and her shoulders lifting with the effort, until it stands roughly vertical. This arc takes well over a full second of screen time — it travels heavily and never flips or snaps open.
4.3-5.0s — the interior is revealed exactly as reference image 3: the neatly folded black LED mesh curtain in its tray with the coiled lead and the small accessory items. She reaches in with both hands and touches the folded mesh, fingers spreading it slightly, then lifts her chin, looks off toward the Christmas tree and breaks into a big open-mouthed grin, eyebrows up.

MOVEMENT RULE FOR BOTH SCENES: she is never frozen and never hurried. Her body is in continuous unhurried motion the whole clip — weight shifting, chest breathing, hair and sleeves swinging and settling, the cushion compressing under the box — and her face keeps changing, eyes, eyebrows and mouth reading differently moment to moment. But every change FLOWS smoothly into the next at natural human speed. She never snaps, never jitters, never stutters between poses.

HARD RULES: exactly ONE cut, at 2.5s. The box never changes size, never changes artwork, never gains a window or a cutout. Nobody else enters frame. NO TEXT, NO LETTERS, NO WORDS, NO NUMBERS, NO CAPTIONS, NO SUBTITLES, NO WATERMARK anywhere in the video.

AUDIO: natural room sound only — no music, no score, no background song. Quiet warm living-room ambience, the soft thump of a heavy box on a cushion, knees on the floor, the click of magnets releasing, stiff cardboard flexing, plastic mesh rustling, one small delighted exhale.

LOOK: real iPhone UGC indoors at night. Warm mixed lamp and fairy light, slight sensor noise in the shadows, natural skin, no cinematic grade, no slow motion, no speed ramp, no fast motion. The whole clip plays at normal 1x speed from first frame to last.

rows.why_html: job 0db96d6f — v21 C2 plus the windowless box packshot, with the over-the-shoulder staging described in words. The camera swung round to her side and the sofa ended up behind her.
job a956d047 — Chained off the take-1 job with “the sofa is directly in front of her” spelled out. Still a side-on room shot.

job c306a101 — Four references, each assigned one job before any description: v20 C2 for the composition, v21 C2 to confirm it, the take-1 job for the woman, the packshot for the box. The written description still overrode all four.

job c11c396a — Reframed as an edit of v21_c02_g1 with every geometric element locked in a list — “if I laid the new image over @Image 1, every edge would land in the same place.” The model pulled the camera back and up into a wide room shot anyway.

job b3ec80ce — A 400-word description of the exact geometry, written after finally opening the reference frames — and still wrong, because the sofa had been read as sitting to her side instead of in front of her.
job bee3b041 — Same double-speed problem as v21 C2.

det.html:
What made it work

Attach the frame and name only what changes. The take that worked is about 110 words: “@Image 1 is the photo. Keep it EXACTLY as it is… CHANGE ONLY TWO THINGS: a different woman, a different room.” Four prompts of 300–450 words describing the same geometry all drifted. Long geometric description competes with the attached reference and wins.

Open the reference before writing about it. Three of those five takes were written from a description of the v20/v21 frame rather than the frame itself. The sofa is in front of her, not beside her — one look would have saved three generations.

What made it work

Speed is a structure problem, not an adjective problem. Piling on “slowly”, “unhurried” and “no fast motion” does nothing while the timeline still asks for three things. The fix was to delete a whole beat and stretch the two survivors to 2.0s each, then add a paragraph that says out loud why the deleted beat is missing: “THAT IS THE WHOLE CLIP… cramming it in is exactly what would force the footage to look sped up.”

“A clearly different pose every half second” is itself a speed-up instruction. That line was in every take-1 prompt and it is what taught the model to snap between poses. It was replaced with a continuous-but-unhurried rule: always moving, never hurried, every change flowing into the next at natural human speed.

Give it permission to end mid-action. “It is far better that she is still mid-reach as the clip ends than that any part of it looks fast-forwarded” removes the model’s incentive to compress, because finishing the action is no longer the goal.

det.text:

det.label: Clip prompt · v22_c03_g2.mp4
det.meta: seedance_2_5 · 720p · 4 s · 9:16 · audio on · job a4c33b88
det.text:
Animate the reference image exactly as it is. The first frame of the video IS the reference image, unchanged — same charcoal board-and-batten wall running away to the LEFT, same gutter and roof edge, same white picket fence, same black folding step stool, same snow on the ground, same woman seen from behind near the RIGHT corner of the wall in the forest-green puffer jacket, standing on the stool with both arms raised pinning the gathered fistful of unlit net up under the gutter, same LED net already hung flat across the wall to her left, same loose tangled coil of curtain heaped on the snow at the bottom left.
REAL TIME — NORMAL 1x SPEED. THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT RULE IN THIS PROMPT. This is one real-time phone video played back at ordinary speed. Everything happens at the pace a real person actually moves: she reaches at the speed an arm really reaches, she shakes the net out at the speed a heavy tangled net really swings, she shifts her weight at the speed a body really balances on a step stool. ABSOLUTELY NO fast motion, NO sped-up playback, NO double speed, NO under-cranking, NO time-lapse, NO hyperlapse, NO sudden jump in tempo, NO frantic twitchy limbs, NO snapping instantly from one pose to the next, NO scrubbing through the action. There is DELIBERATELY very little to do in four seconds — one slow shake, one slow reach, one slow sideways press. If the action does not fit comfortably, SLOW THE ACTION DOWN; never speed the footage up. It is far better that she is still mid-reach as the clip ends than that any part of it looks fast-forwarded.

CAMERA — HELD IPHONE, LOCKED FOCAL LENGTH. A low three-quarter angle from the snow, portrait, exactly the framing of the reference image with the wall receding hard to the left. Handheld micro-shake only — a few pixels of organic drift. ABSOLUTELY NO ZOOM IN, NO ZOOM OUT, NO PUSH IN, NO PULL BACK, NO DOLLY, NO CRANE, NO ORBIT. The wall, the roof edge, the picket fence and the stool stay exactly the same size in frame from the first frame to the last.

MOVEMENT RULE: she is never frozen and never hurried. Her body is in continuous unhurried motion the whole four seconds — weight shifting on the stool, shoulders rolling, ribs breathing, hair swinging and settling, the puffer jacket creasing and rustling, the strands swaying on after every touch. But every change FLOWS smoothly into the next at natural human speed. She never snaps, never jitters, never stutters between poses, and no limb ever travels faster than a real arm travels.

ACTION TIMELINE (4 seconds, one continuous take, no cuts) — ONLY TWO THINGS HAPPEN, AND BOTH ARE SLOW:
0.0-2.0s — she lifts the gathered bundle in her right hand and shakes it out ONCE, slowly and heavily. The shake takes well over a full second of screen time: her arm swings out and down, the tangled net lets go in stages rather than all at once, and a long sheet of strands falls open down the dark battens and swings for a moment before it settles. The loose coil on the snow drags and shifts with it.
2.0-4.0s — still up on the stool, she stretches both arms high and presses the header wire up under the lip of the gutter, her thumbs working slowly along it, then walks her hands a short way sideways to her LEFT along the roofline, pressing and tucking as she goes, her torso twisting and her heels lifting and dropping on the tread. She is STILL tucking when the clip ends. The curtain sways gently against the battens and is still settling on the last frame.
THAT IS THE WHOLE CLIP. She does NOT step down off the stool, does NOT step back, does NOT plant her hands on her hips and does NOT tilt her head back to look at her work. There is no time for any of that at real speed, and cramming it in is exactly what would force the footage to look sped up. She stays on the stool from the first frame to the last.

HARD RULES: the curtain is COMPLETELY OFF the entire time — not one bulb lights, no glow, no colour, no animation on the wall. The wall never gains windows, doors or new features and the picket fence never changes. The strands are separate vertical strands obeying gravity, sagging slightly, with an uneven wavy bottom hem — never a flat sheet, never a panel, never a screen. The loose coil rests in the snow with real contact shadows. Her face is never shown; she stays turned away from camera throughout. No other people enter frame. NO TEXT, NO LETTERS, NO WORDS, NO NUMBERS, NO CAPTIONS, NO SUBTITLES, NO WATERMARK anywhere in the video.

AUDIO: natural room sound only — no music, no score, no background song. Cold outdoor winter ambience, thin plastic strands rattling and clicking against wood siding, a step-stool creak, sneakers on a metal tread, boots compressing snow, one quiet effortful breath. No voice.

LOOK: real iPhone UGC. Flat overcast winter daylight, slightly cool white balance, mild sensor noise, natural skin, no cinematic grade, no lens flare, no slow motion, no speed ramp, no fast motion. The whole clip plays at normal 1x speed from first frame to last.

rows.why_html: job 02aa808f — Same double-speed problem as v21 C3 — three action beats in four seconds.

det.html:
What made it work

Speed is a structure problem, not an adjective problem. Piling on “slowly”, “unhurried” and “no fast motion” does nothing while the timeline still asks for three things. The fix was to delete a whole beat and stretch the two survivors to 2.0s each, then add a paragraph that says out loud why the deleted beat is missing: “THAT IS THE WHOLE CLIP… cramming it in is exactly what would force the footage to look sped up.”

“A clearly different pose every half second” is itself a speed-up instruction. That line was in every take-1 prompt and it is what taught the model to snap between poses. It was replaced with a continuous-but-unhurried rule: always moving, never hurried, every change flowing into the next at natural human speed.

Give it permission to end mid-action. “It is far better that she is still mid-reach as the clip ends than that any part of it looks fast-forwarded” removes the model’s incentive to compress, because finishing the action is no longer the goal.

ABSOLUTE FIRST RULE — THE LIT PICTURE IS TRAPPED INSIDE THE CURTAIN RECTANGLE. In the reference image the lit LED curtain is a rectangle hanging across the garage door only, and it stops short of the door's edges. That rectangle is FIXED for the whole four seconds: it never grows, never widens, never rises, never rescales, never warps, never drifts, and the camera never changes size on it. The reindeer, the sleigh, the presents and the snowman are drawn INSIDE that rectangle with a clear band of unlit dark door left all the way round — a generous margin at the top, and margins at the left, right and bottom.
NOTHING LIT EVER CROSSES AN EDGE. No hoof, no antler, no rein, no runner of the sleigh, no present and no stick arm ever touches or crosses the edge of the curtain, and nothing lit ever appears on the siding, the basketball hoop, the gables, the roof, the sky or the neighbouring house. If a pose would take a limb or a prop out to an edge, THE POSE IS MADE SMALLER so it stays inside — the rectangle is never made bigger to fit it. The garage door outside the curtain, and every surface around it, stays dark the whole four seconds.

CAMERA — HELD IPHONE, LOCKED FRAMING. Portrait, filmed from behind the group at the bottom of the driveway. Handheld micro-shake only — a few pixels of organic drift. ABSOLUTELY NO ZOOM IN, NO ZOOM OUT, NO PUSH IN, NO PULL BACK, NO DOLLY, NO CRANE. The house, the basketball hoop and the garage door stay exactly the same size in frame from the first frame to the last.

THE CROWD IS CASUAL, RELAXED AND ALREADY HAPPY — AND ALREADY MOVING IN THE VERY FIRST FRAME. This is not an audience waiting for something to happen. Nobody is standing frozen staring at the garage in anticipation, nobody holds still and then reacts, there is no build-up and no big synchronised cheer. They are neighbours hanging about on a driveway on a cold night, chatting to each other, laughing at each other, sipping drinks, glancing over at the lights and then back at their friends. Their attention drifts on and off the garage the whole time. They are ALL seen FROM BEHIND — no face is ever turned toward camera.
AT 0.0s, IN THE VERY FIRST FRAME, EVERY PERSON IS ALREADY MID-MOVEMENT. There is NO still opening frame, NO frozen first beat, NO pause before the motion starts, NO moment where the group holds and waits. Someone is already mid-laugh, someone is already turning, someone is already raising a cup, a child is already bouncing. The clip starts in the middle of the action and never settles.
CONTINUOUS OVERLAPPING MOTION, EVERY HALF SECOND, NEVER IN UNISON — at any instant several different people are doing several different things, and their little actions start and stop at different times so the group always looks alive:
0.0-0.5s — a child near the front is already bouncing on the spot and swings an arm up toward the garage mid-bounce; two adults beside them are mid-conversation, heads turned to each other, one shrugging.
0.5-1.0s — a woman in the centre laughs and rocks back on her heels, shoulders shaking; a man at the right is already filming on his phone and shifts his weight to his other foot; someone lifts a takeaway cup and drinks.
1.0-1.5s — the kids sitting in the front row lean into each other and one points lazily at the lights without turning round; a teenager at the left shoves both hands deeper into their pockets, hunches, and blows out a long fog of breath.
1.5-2.0s — a woman at the left leans sideways into the person beside her and says something; they both laugh; another person scratches under their bobble hat and looks away from the garage entirely.
2.0-2.5s — two people knock shoulders and one claps once, casually; a child in a bobble hat twists round to tug a sleeve, then swings back; a couple sway slightly, arms linked.
2.5-3.0s — scattered easy laughter ripples through the group, a few loose claps at different moments, not together; one adult crouches down to say something to a kid; another points out at the lights with a cup still in hand.
3.0-3.5s — the man at the right lowers his phone, wipes his eyes laughing and says something sideways; a kid scrambles up onto their knees; two heads tip together.
3.5-4.0s — a few people applaud loosely, hats bobbing, breath fogging, someone waves an arm overhead at a neighbour, someone else is already turning to talk to the person behind them.
Coats crease, hats bob, breath fogs, snow compresses under boots, shoulders shake with laughter. NOBODY IS EVER STILL and nobody is waiting.

THE ARTWORK IS ALREADY ANIMATING IN THE FIRST FRAME — it is mid-cycle at 0.0s, not switching on and not holding still, and it changes again at 0.2s. THE ARTWORK ANIMATES THROUGHOUT, in its own beats, redrawing fully between them: at 0.2s and again at 0.6s the reindeer's legs extend into a full gallop stride, front hooves reaching far forward, mane and tail streaming back; at 1.4s the stack of presents in the sleigh shifts hard and the top one tumbles off the back and drops away; at 2.2s the reindeer's red nose flashes to double brightness and back, its head thrown up and antlers tipping; at 3.0s the snowman's raised stick arm sweeps down and up in a big wave and he hops off the ground, his hat bouncing; at 3.6s the reindeer rears, both front hooves in the air, the sleigh tipping up at the front and the reins snapping tight. The coloured reflections on the wet driveway shift and ripple with every change.

The picture on the garage door is NOT an LED video wall, NOT a screen, NOT a projection. Build the whole picture out of VERTICAL DOTTED LINES OF LIGHT. The horizontal gap between neighbouring strands is visibly WIDER than the vertical gap between bulbs on the same strand, so the grid is tall and rectangular — never a square pixel matrix.
The curtain is SEE-THROUGH. Through the gaps between strands you clearly read the garage door behind it: its horizontal panel seams, its rim of trim, the faint shadows of the wires falling on it. Light spills onto the snow in a speckled uneven pattern, not a flat even wash.
ABSOLUTELY NO: LED video wall, TV screen, monitor, jumbotron, projector image, black backing panel, bezel or frame, dense square pixel grid, solid saturated background field, smooth clean vector artwork. Real amateur photo, natural noise, no CGI polish.

ABSOLUTE HARD RULE — THE GARAGE DOOR IS THE ONLY LIT SURFACE. The artwork is hard-cropped at all four edges of the curtain. It NEVER grows, shrinks, shifts, warps or drifts. Nothing spills onto the siding, the basketball hoop, the gables, the roof, the sky or the neighbouring house. No hoof, antler or stick arm ever crosses outside the curtain rectangle.

det.html:
File name

The old board listed v22_c06_g2.mp4 as the clip in the cut and marked it lost. This take is on disk as v22_c06_g1.mp4: its Higgsfield job carries the same clip prompt and its frames match the export (checked 2026-09-23). The 2026-09-18 naming migration left it under the earlier take number.

What made it work

The blocky-grid block and the beautiful-artwork block cannot both be in one prompt. They pull in opposite directions and the blocky one wins. g2 drops the “low resolution, chunky stepped edges, no smooth curves” paragraph and uses the C5/C7 wording instead — “DENSELY spaced, many small round bulbs closely spaced along it, so the curtain has plenty of resolution” — while keeping every see-through rule.

What made it work

A crowd that waits and then reacts always looks staged. The rewrite bans the build-up outright: they are neighbours hanging about, chatting to each other, glancing at the lights and back at their friends, attention drifting on and off the garage the whole time.

Start the clip mid-action, explicitly at 0.0s. “AT 0.0s, IN THE VERY FIRST FRAME, EVERY PERSON IS ALREADY MID-MOVEMENT” plus named examples (already mid-laugh, already turning, already raising a cup) removes the frozen opening beat.

Stagger the beats so nothing happens in unison. Half-second rows, each naming two or three different people doing unrelated things, produce a group that reads as alive rather than choreographed.

NO zoom in, NO zoom out, NO push-in, NO pull-back, NO pan, NO tilt, NO dolly, NO orbit, NO digital crop, NO cuts, NO slow motion, NO speed ramp. The roof, the ladder and the garage stay exactly the same size in frame from the first frame to the last. The only camera movement is handheld micro-shake, plus one small startled jolt at the moment he goes over.

ACTION TIMELINE — HE LOSES IT AND GOES OVER THE EDGE (5 seconds, one continuous take):
0.0-1.2s — he is genuinely struggling, hauling on an orange ratchet strap with both fists, boots braced wide on the shingles; the faded Santa figure flops and slides sideways, its arm swinging loose, the bulb strings snagging round his wrist and his boot; his shoulders heave, his breath fogs, his puffer jacket bunches and creases.

2.0-3.0s — he goes down hard on his backside and slides fast down the pitch toward the gutter, boots-first, hands scrabbling at the shingles and finding nothing, mouth wide open in a panicked yell, the Santa figure dragged along behind him on the tangled strings.
3.0-4.0s — he shoots off the edge past the gutter, limbs flailing, his mustard beanie flying off, still screaming, and drops out of the bottom of the composition behind the ladder into the deep snow with a heavy muffled WHUMP and an explosion of powder. The ladder rattles hard against the eave but does NOT fall.
4.0-5.0s — the cloud of powder drifts and settles; the Santa figure slithers off the roof a second later and flops down after him; loose snow slides off the shingles in a small sheet; the bulb strings swing and settle; everything goes still.

MOVEMENT RULE: a clearly different whole-body pose every half second. No beat is static. Jacket creases, snow sprays, strings whip, breath fogs.

HARD RULES: this is a stuntman-style comedy pratfall — clumsy, harmless and funny. He lands in deep soft powder. NO blood, NO injury, NO gore, nothing broken. He NEVER turns to camera and his face is never held in close-up. Nobody else is in shot, nobody walks in, nobody helps him. NOT ONE LED bulb is lit at any point — the strings are completely dark all five seconds. The operator never walks forward, never follows him down, never lowers the camera to look at him. DO NOT CHANGE the roof, the brick garage, the white neighbour house, the ladder position, the parked black pickup, the snow line, the sky or the exposure. NO TEXT, NO LETTERS, NO WORDS, NO NUMBERS, NO CAPTIONS, NO SUBTITLES, NO WATERMARK anywhere in the video.

AUDIO: natural room sound only — no music, no score, no background song. A ratchet strap clacking, stiff plastic crackling, boots scraping hard on shingles, an aluminium ladder rattling against the eave, his loud panicked yell, then a heavy muffled thump into deep snow and silence. Nobody speaks, no narration.

LOOK: real iPhone UGC. Flat overcast winter daylight, slightly cool white balance, mild sensor noise, mild rolling-shutter wobble on the fast motion, no bokeh, no cinematic grade, no lens flare, no slow motion, no speed ramp.

job 31d9e148 — Collapsed reindeer with one antler folded flat, forest-green clapboard, wood-look garage door. The flopped antler is the funniest detail of the three, but the dark green wall swallows the decoration at this distance.

det.html:
What made it work

Three options, one camera, one paragraph of change each. All three attach the same v16 C1 frame and keep the camera paragraph word for word; only the HOUSE and DECORATION paragraphs differ. That is why the three options are directly comparable — Daniel is choosing a decoration, not re-judging a shot. Option C won on contrast: the bleached white Santa face against a black garage door reads instantly at thumbnail size.

Say what the man is NOT doing. “NOT falling and NOT off balance … BOTH BOOTS PLANTED FLAT on the shingles” is in all three prompts. Without it, “man on a roof” keeps generating a slapstick fall, which is a different ad.

det.label: Clip prompt · v23_c02_g2.mp4
det.text:
TWO SCENES IN ONE CLIP, JOINED BY ONE HARD CUT AT EXACTLY 2.5s. No dissolve, no fade, no whip pan, no transition effect — a straight in-camera cut, exactly like a creator cutting two takes together.

REAL TIME — NORMAL 1x SPEED. THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT RULE IN THIS PROMPT. This is one real-time phone video played back at ordinary speed. Everything happens at the pace a real person actually moves: she walks at a walking pace, she kneels at the speed a body really kneels, the lid swings open at the speed heavy cardboard really swings. ABSOLUTELY NO fast motion, NO sped-up playback, NO double speed, NO under-cranking, NO time-lapse, NO hyperlapse, NO sudden jump in tempo, NO frantic twitchy limbs, NO snapping instantly from one pose to the next, NO scrubbing through the action. There is DELIBERATELY very little to do in five seconds — one slow lowering, one slow kneel, one slow lid. If the action does not fit comfortably, SLOW THE ACTION DOWN; never speed the footage up. It is far better that she is still settling as the clip ends than that any part of it looks fast-forwarded.

REFERENCE IMAGES. Reference image 1 is the first frame of scene 1 — start there, unchanged, and it owns the room, the camera angle and the geometry. Reference image 2 is the CLOSED PRODUCT BOX: the artwork on the box in this video must match it exactly. Reference image 3 is the OPEN BOX INTERIOR: what she reveals in scene 2 must match it exactly.

BOX SPEC — TRUE IN EVERY FRAME. A matte black rigid retail box, 55 cm wide x 42 cm tall x 10 cm deep. It is BIG — much wider than the span of two outstretched hands; each of her hands covers less than a quarter of the box width, and laid on the sofa seat it spans most of one cushion. Front panel top to bottom: a large white condensed uppercase headline LED CURTAIN LIGHTS; a warm gold subline Create Your Own Magic; a red diagonal BEST SELLER ribbon flag in the top-right corner; one large photographic panel with a thin gold hairline border showing a night house facade with a glowing pixel LED Christmas tree on the garage door; a bottom row of five small gold line icons with white captions. NO transparent window, NO clear plastic panel, NO die-cut cutout, NO product visible through the front, NO glowing lights showing through the cardboard. The box is closed and sealed until the moment she opens it in scene 2.

SCENE 1 — 0.0 to 2.5s. CAMERA: HELD IPHONE, LOCKED FOCAL LENGTH, portrait, a friend filming from above head height over her left shoulder and angled down, exactly where the reference image was taken. NO ZOOM IN, NO ZOOM OUT, NO PUSH IN, NO DOLLY. Handheld micro-shake only. She is at the LEFT EDGE of frame, partly cut off by it; the teal velvet sofa is directly IN FRONT of her, running diagonally away into depth and filling the right and bottom-right of frame. The room behind her — the Christmas tree with its multicolour bulbs, the brass lamp, the wall and the floor — stays exactly as it is and never changes.
THE WHOLE POINT OF SCENE 1: she carries the box round in front of the sofa, sets it flat on the seat cushion AND drops to her knees IN THE SAME CONTINUOUS MOTION. These are not two separate steps — the box going down and her body going down are one move.
0.0-0.9s — one unhurried step forward and to her right, her shoulders turning, the heavy box swinging slowly out in front of her; her copper-auburn hair swings across and settles, her blush sweater sleeve creases with the weight.
0.9-1.8s — she steps in front of the sofa and leans forward from the hips, lowering the box steadily toward the empty teal velvet seat cushion, arms extending, knees already bending underneath her. This lowering is SLOW and heavy — the box is big and awkward and she is being careful with it.
1.8-2.5s — the box settles flat and printed-side-up on the cushion with a soft compression of the velvet, her hands still on it, and in the same continuous motion her knees come down onto the floor one after the other, her weight settling and her back rounding forward; she pushes her hair behind one ear and plants both palms flat on the box lid, chest rising with one excited breath.

HARD CUT AT 2.5s.

SCENE 2 — 2.5 to 5.0s. Direct continuation, same room, same second, same woman, same blush sweater, same box in exactly the same place on the same teal velvet cushion. The camera has moved about 30 degrees round to her side — a slightly more side-on three-quarter angle, a little lower, closer to the level of the sofa seat, so we now see the lid edge in profile and read the pivot clearly. Still HELD IPHONE, LOCKED FOCAL LENGTH, handheld micro-shake only, NO ZOOM.
LID MECHANISM, GEOMETRICALLY. The box is a magnetic-closure flip-top. The hinge runs along the TOP LONG EDGE of the box — the far edge away from her, at the back. The lid pivots UP and BACK on that hinge, rotating away from her and toward the back of the sofa, keeping its printed front face turned toward the camera as it rises. The inside of the lid is matte black. The lid is NEVER lifted off, NEVER removed, NEVER carried aside, NEVER set down, NEVER folded flat instantly, NEVER slid out like a drawer.
2.5-3.1s — she hooks her fingertips under the near front edge of the lid; a small snap as the magnets release and the front edge lifts a centimetre, a thin black shadow line opening slowly across the whole 55 cm width.
3.1-4.3s — she pivots the big printed lid UP and BACK on its hinge in ONE slow continuous arc with real cardboard weight, her elbows rising and her shoulders lifting with the effort, until it stands roughly vertical. This arc takes well over a full second of screen time — it travels heavily and never flips or snaps open.
4.3-5.0s — the interior is revealed exactly as reference image 3: the neatly folded black LED mesh curtain in its tray with the coiled lead and the small accessory items. She reaches in with both hands and touches the folded mesh, fingers spreading it slightly, then lifts her chin, looks off toward the Christmas tree and breaks into a big open-mouthed grin, eyebrows up.

MOVEMENT RULE FOR BOTH SCENES: she is never frozen and never hurried. Her body is in continuous unhurried motion the whole clip — weight shifting, chest breathing, hair and sleeves swinging and settling, the cushion compressing under the box — and her face keeps changing, eyes, eyebrows and mouth reading differently moment to moment. But every change FLOWS smoothly into the next at natural human speed. She never snaps, never jitters, never stutters between poses.

HARD RULES: exactly ONE cut, at 2.5s. The box never changes size, never changes artwork, never gains a window or a cutout. Nobody else enters frame. NO TEXT, NO LETTERS, NO WORDS, NO NUMBERS, NO CAPTIONS, NO SUBTITLES, NO WATERMARK anywhere in the video.

AUDIO: natural room sound only — no music, no score, no background song. Quiet warm living-room ambience, the soft thump of a heavy box on a cushion, knees on the floor, the click of magnets releasing, stiff cardboard flexing, plastic mesh rustling, one small delighted exhale.
